status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: High pole is consistently 'more collection / less privacy protection'.

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of government monitoring of phone and internet records?
items.scope: Monitoring to find terrorists and spies, under any administration: for example, collecting records of who calls or emails whom, when and for how long, for millions of Americans at once.

sides.label: Protect privacy
sides.text: Limit monitoring, even if it makes some attacks harder to stop.

sides.label: Prioritize security
sides.text: Allow broad monitoring, even if many innocent people's records are collected.

items.stem: When intelligence agencies want to read Americans' messages, which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Messages of people in the US, collected in security investigations.

sides.label: Warrant first
sides.text: They should get a judge's warrant first, even if that slows investigations.

sides.label: Collect, then check
sides.text: They should be able to collect first and get approval later, so threats aren't missed.

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of security cameras and license plate readers run by cities and police?
items.scope: Cameras in public places like streets and parks.

sides.label: Fewer cameras
sides.text: Limit them, even if some crimes go unsolved.

sides.label: More cameras
sides.text: Use them widely, even if everyone's movements are recorded.

items.stem: Should tech companies be required to give police a way to unlock encrypted phones and messages when a court orders it?
items.scope: Encryption scrambles data so only the owner can read it. Any unlock method could also be found by hackers.
options: No; strong encryption that no one can unlock protects everyone
Only in the most serious cases, such as terrorism or child exploitation
Yes, in any criminal case with a court order

items.stem: Should police be allowed to use facial recognition software to identify people from photos and video?
items.scope: Think of ordinary police work. Specific situations come next.
options: Only to identify suspects in serious crimes, with a warrant
Yes, including live scanning of crowds in public places

items.stem: Under the rule you chose, should police be able to use it in each of these situations?

cases.text: Identifying a suspect in a terrorist attack, without a warrant
Identifying people at a protest where some property was damaged

items.stem: Should there be a federal law limiting what companies can do with personal data they collect online?
items.scope: Data like location, browsing and purchases.
options: Yes, strict: companies need your permission before collecting or selling it
Yes, moderate: you can tell companies not to sell it
No federal law; leave it to states
No new laws; people can choose which services to use

items.stem: Should government agencies be allowed to buy personal data, such as phone location history, from companies without a warrant?
items.scope: Data about people in the US that companies sell commercially.
options: Yes, if the data is for sale to anyone

items.stem: Should the US create a national digital ID that people use to prove who they are online and in person?
items.scope: It would be issued by the federal government and work on a phone.
options: No; keep using state IDs and passports

items.subtopic: Searches of phones at the border
items.stem: Should border agents be able to search the phones and laptops of people entering the US?
items.scope: Applies to US citizens coming home and to visitors.
items.context: Under current rules, agents can look through a device without any suspicion; copying its data requires reasonable suspicion.
options: Only with reasonable suspicion of a crime
Yes, for any traveler, as current rules mostly allow

facts.claim: CBP basic device searches need no suspicion; advanced (forensic) searches need reasonable suspicion or national security concern

items.stem: Should police be able to search consumer DNA databases, like ancestry sites, to find suspects through their relatives?
items.scope: Sites where people upload their DNA to find family.
options: Only with a warrant, for violent crimes

items.stem: Should employers be allowed to monitor workers' computers, keystrokes and locations during work hours?
options: No, only with the worker's agreement for specific reasons
Yes, but they must tell workers exactly what is monitored
Yes, freely; it's the employer's equipment and time
